ah_in_use.explanation: IPsec has two protocols for protecting packets. AH authenticates a packet and parts of its outer header but provides no confidentiality whatsoever; ESP can provide both, and is what essentially all modern deployments use. Seeing AH is therefore worth noting — it may be deliberate, since AH covers some outer-header fields that ESP does not, but far more often it is a legacy configuration. This is flagged as informational rather than as a vulnerability. Detection is simply the IP protocol number on the wire, so it is directly observed.
ah_in_use.recommendation: AH provides integrity but no confidentiality and is largely superseded by ESP (which can provide both). Migrate to ESP unless AH's specific properties (e.g. protecting outer IP header fields) are a hard requirement.
ah_in_use.title: AH in use (deprecated)

anti_replay_not_observable.explanation: Anti-replay protection means a receiver refuses packets it has already seen, so an attacker cannot capture traffic and replay it later. The sequence number this relies on is present in every ESP packet whether or not the receiver actually checks it — enforcement is a decision made inside the receiving host and is never signalled on the wire. No passive observer can determine it, from this capture or any other, and a tool that reports it is guessing. This is the clearest example of why the report distinguishes "we could not tell" from "it is fine": here, "could not tell" is the only truthful answer available.
anti_replay_not_observable.passed_title: Anti-replay window enforcement observed as enabled
anti_replay_not_observable.recommendation: Anti-replay window enforcement is a receiver-side policy decision never signaled on the wire — the sequence number is present in every ESP packet regardless of whether the receiver checks it. Verify directly against both endpoints' configuration.
anti_replay_not_observable.title: Anti-replay window enforcement: never observable from a passive capture

downgrade_exposure_hybrid_pq.explanation: A hybrid post-quantum deployment (RFC 9370) runs an additional post-quantum key exchange alongside the classical one, so that traffic recorded today cannot be decrypted later by a quantum computer. The weakness this check looks for is specific and unintuitive: if the handshake is not protected against tampering, an on-path attacker can strip the extra exchange out and leave a classical-only negotiation, and neither end will notice. The organisation has paid for post-quantum migration and is still exposed to precisely the attack that migration was meant to address, which is why this is treated as the most serious downgrade exposure.
downgrade_exposure_hybrid_pq.recommendation: A hybrid post-quantum key exchange without full downgrade protection can be silently stripped back to classical-only KEX by an on-path attacker; ensure both peers send notify 16447.
downgrade_exposure_hybrid_pq.title: Downgrade exposure: hybrid post-quantum deployment without full protection

downgrade_exposure_mixed_strength.explanation: An IKEv2 initiator offers a list of key-exchange groups and the responder picks one. If that list mixes weak groups with strong ones, an attacker sitting on the path can tamper with the offer so the two ends settle on the weakest option, while both sides believe they simply negotiated normally. A newer IKEv2 extension (notify type 16447) lets both peers authenticate the whole handshake transcript afterwards, which makes such tampering detectable. This check fires when a mixed-strength offer is made *and* that protection is not fully in place. Both the offered groups and the notify are plaintext, so this is directly observed.
downgrade_exposure_mixed_strength.passed_title: Key-exchange proposal does not mix weak and strong DH groups
downgrade_exposure_mixed_strength.recommendation: Remove weak DH groups from the proposal entirely, or ensure both peers send the full-transcript-authentication notify (16447) so a downgrade attempt is detectable.
downgrade_exposure_mixed_strength.title: Downgrade exposure: proposal mixes weak and strong DH groups

downgrade_exposure_weak_group_negotiable.explanation: This is the milder relative of the mixed-strength check. Here a weak key-exchange group appears in the offer but was not the one finally selected, and full handshake protection is not in place. The connection you are looking at is not itself using the weak group — but the option remains on the table, and an attacker able to tamper with the negotiation could steer a future handshake onto it. Removing an unused weak group from the proposal costs nothing and closes the door. Both the offer and the protection state are plaintext, so this is directly observed.
downgrade_exposure_weak_group_negotiable.passed_title: No weak DH group left negotiable
downgrade_exposure_weak_group_negotiable.recommendation: Remove the weak DH group from the proposal, even though it wasn't the one ultimately selected — it remains available to a downgrade attempt.
downgrade_exposure_weak_group_negotiable.title: Downgrade exposure: a weak DH group remains negotiable

ikev1_aggressive_mode.explanation: IKEv1 offers two ways to run its first phase. Main Mode protects the peers' identities; Aggressive Mode compresses the exchange into fewer round trips and sends identity information in the clear — and, when pre-shared-key authentication is used, a hash derived from that shared key along with it. Anyone who records the exchange can then attack that hash offline, guessing passwords at their own pace with nothing to detect the attempt. IKEv2 has no Aggressive Mode exchange type at all, so on an IKEv2 capture this check is structurally not applicable rather than merely absent.
ikev1_aggressive_mode.passed_title: IKEv1 Aggressive Mode not in use
ikev1_aggressive_mode.recommendation: Disable Aggressive Mode; it exposes the peer identity (and, with PSK authentication, a hash usable for offline dictionary attacks) in the clear. Use Main Mode or migrate to IKEv2.
ikev1_aggressive_mode.title: IKEv1 Aggressive Mode in use

ikev1_in_use.explanation: IKEv1 is the original key-exchange protocol for IPsec and has been formally deprecated (RFC 9395) in favour of IKEv2. Deprecated does not mean broken on its own, but it does mean the protocol no longer receives scrutiny or new protections, and IKEv1 deployments tend to be old configurations nobody has revisited. Worth knowing: this tool reports more about IKEv1 than IKEv2 in one respect, because IKEv1 Main Mode leaves more of the negotiation in the clear. It does not attempt IKEv1 SA-parameter extraction. The version number is read from the IKE header.
ikev1_in_use.recommendation: Migrate to IKEv2; IKEv1 is deprecated (RFC 9395) and SA-parameter extraction was not attempted for it.
ikev1_in_use.title: IKEv1 in use

null_encryption.explanation: ESP can be configured with a NULL cipher, meaning the packets carry their integrity tag but no confidentiality at all — the payload travels in the clear inside what looks like an encrypted tunnel. This is a legitimate setting for debugging a deployment and is never appropriate for real traffic. Because it is so serious, this tool will not assert it from packet sizes alone: it reads a sample of the payload bytes and asks whether they actually parse as a plain IP header. Real encrypted traffic is indistinguishable from random noise and essentially never does, so NULL encryption is ruled out unless there is positive evidence for it.
null_encryption.passed_title: NULL encryption ruled out for ESP
null_encryption.recommendation: This traffic has no confidentiality protection at all. Confirm this is intentional (e.g. a debugging/testing deployment) and never route production traffic through it unencrypted.
null_encryption.title: NULL encryption in use for ESP

partial_downgrade_protection.explanation: Protection against handshake tampering (notify type 16447) only works if *both* peers support it, and that makes a simple yes/no check misleading. A responder sends the notify whenever it supports the feature, regardless of whether the initiator did — so seeing it in the response tells you nothing on its own. There are four possible states: both sent it (protected), neither did (no protection), or exactly one did. This check fires on those one-sided cases and names which end is missing it, because that is the endpoint somebody has to go and upgrade.
partial_downgrade_protection.recommendation: {value} does not send the full-transcript-authentication notify (16447); protection requires both peers to send it. Upgrade the deficient endpoint's IKE implementation.
partial_downgrade_protection.title: Partial downgrade protection: {value} does not support it

pfs_not_observable.explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy means each tunnel gets a freshly agreed key, so that compromising one key later does not expose traffic protected by the others. Whether it is enabled is signalled by a key-exchange payload inside the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange — which this build does not parse. That is a limitation of this tool, not of passive analysis: the information is present on the wire and a future version could read it. Until then this check reports honestly that it does not know, rather than assuming a default. Verify it against both endpoints' configuration directly.
pfs_not_observable.passed_title: Perfect Forward Secrecy observed as enabled
pfs_not_observable.recommendation: PFS is signaled by a KE payload in CREATE_CHILD_SA, which this MVP does not parse (out of scope). Verify PFS configuration directly against both endpoints' policy.
pfs_not_observable.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy: not observable from this capture

sixty_four_bit_block_cipher_in_esp.explanation: Block ciphers encrypt in fixed-size chunks. Older ciphers — 3DES, DES, Blowfish, CAST — use a 64-bit block, and with a block that small, repeated blocks start showing up once enough data has been sent under one key, purely by the mathematics of coincidence. That leakage is the basis of the Sweet32 class of attacks, and the data volumes involved are ordinary for a busy VPN rather than theoretical. This tool does not decrypt anything: it recovers the cipher's block alignment from the *sizes* of the encrypted packets, which is why this finding is labelled as inferred from a side channel rather than observed.
sixty_four_bit_block_cipher_in_esp.passed_title: No 64-bit block cipher family in ESP
sixty_four_bit_block_cipher_in_esp.recommendation: 64-bit block ciphers (3DES/DES/Blowfish/CAST) are vulnerable to birthday-bound attacks (e.g. Sweet32) well within realistic traffic volumes. Migrate to an AES-based AEAD suite.
sixty_four_bit_block_cipher_in_esp.title: 64-bit block cipher family in use for ESP

truncated_96_bit_icv.explanation: Every ESP packet carries an integrity check value — a short tag proving the packet was not altered in transit. Some older transforms truncate that tag to 96 bits. That remains permitted by the standards and is not break-today weak, but it leaves a smaller margin than the 128-bit and longer tags modern suites use, and there is rarely a reason to prefer it now. The tag length is recovered by arithmetic on observed packet sizes, anchored on packets whose true size is structurally forced, so it is labelled as inferred from a side channel rather than observed.
truncated_96_bit_icv.recommendation: A 96-bit truncated MAC remains standards-permitted but offers a smaller security margin than 128-bit+ alternatives (e.g. HMAC-SHA-256-128, AES-GCM's 128-bit tag); prefer those where supported.
truncated_96_bit_icv.title: Truncated 96-bit integrity check value

weak_dh_group_negotiated.explanation: Diffie-Hellman is how the two ends agree on a shared secret while somebody is watching the wire. The "group" is the mathematical setting that agreement happens in, and it decides how hard the secret is to work out from the outside. Groups 1, 2 and 5 use small prime moduli (768, 1024 and 1536 bits); groups 22 to 24 pair a modulus with a small-order subgroup. All six are deprecated for current use. The practical worry is recorded traffic: an attacker who stores today's handshake may be able to break it later. The negotiated group travels in the clear in IKE_SA_INIT, so this is read straight off the wire rather than inferred.
weak_dh_group_negotiated.recommendation: Negotiate DH group 14 (2048-bit MODP) or higher, or an ECP group (19-21), instead of the weak group in use.
weak_dh_group_negotiated.title: Weak Diffie-Hellman group negotiated

weak_ike_sa_cipher.explanation: This is about the cipher protecting the *key-exchange conversation* itself, not the tunnelled traffic. DES has been breakable by brute force for decades, and 3DES inherits the 64-bit block problem described under the ESP block-cipher check while being slow besides; current guidance (RFC 8247) recommends against both. It matters because the IKE SA is where identities are exchanged and where the keys for the data tunnel are derived. The negotiated cipher appears in the plaintext IKE_SA_INIT exchange, so this is read directly rather than inferred.
weak_ike_sa_cipher.recommendation: DES and 3DES are cryptographically weak by modern standards (RFC 8247 recommends against them). Migrate the IKE SA to an AES-based cipher.
weak_ike_sa_cipher.title: Weak IKE SA cipher (DES / 3DES)

weak_ike_sa_integrity.explanation: The integrity transform is what stops anyone tampering with the key-exchange messages themselves. Transforms built on MD5 and SHA-1 are deprecated (RFC 8247): both hash functions have known collision weaknesses, and while a collision is not automatically an attack on the authentication code built from them, there is no reason to keep relying on primitives that have been failing for years. SHA-2-based transforms are the current recommendation. Like the cipher, this is negotiated in the clear in IKE_SA_INIT and read directly.
weak_ike_sa_integrity.passed_title: No weak IKE SA integrity (MD5 / SHA-1)
weak_ike_sa_integrity.recommendation: MD5- and SHA-1-based integrity transforms are deprecated (RFC 8247). Migrate the IKE SA to a SHA-2-based integrity transform (e.g. HMAC-SHA2-256-128).
weak_ike_sa_integrity.title: Weak IKE SA integrity (MD5 / SHA-1)
